Yes, that's fair. I used an AI coding assistant to help prepare this PR, and I should have said so up front.

I didn't want to hand you an unchecked bulk edit, so here's what was verified before opening it:
1. Only keys that are real `ManimConfig` properties were converted. Places where `config` is a local dict or a `ConfigParser` were left alone.
2.  `__getitem__` is `getattr` and `__setitem__` calls the property setter, so runtime behavior is identical.
3. mypy reports 285 errors on `main` and 285 on t

Generally, it's ok to use AI for contributing. We just like keeping beginner-level issues for people who want to start contributing, and the use of AI works against that.

So thanks for your contribution. But since this isn't a critical change, I will close this PR in favor of letting somebody else have a simple entry for contribution.

I appreciate the honesty with your disclaimer, but don't really feel that we should get a solution not well understood merged, especially if it constitutes a breaking change.

I'm quite certain that there is a cleaner solution; the current behavior is likely because the miter type is a class and not a instance variable (or is it?) -- if you are willing to spend some more time figuring this out, then I'm happy to take a closer look at your proposal as well.

Understood! I'm hoping that this will be seen by someone with knowledge of the history that led to the current code. That said, I believe I understand the issue.

`LineJointType` and `CapStyleType` are simply enums. They are both mapped to Cairo constants in `camera.py` - see `LINE_JOIN_MAP` and `CAP_STYLE_MAP`. Both these dictionaries map the `AUTO` values to `None`. These dictionaries are only used in `Camera.apply_stroke()`, where they update the Cairo context:
```python
ctx.set_line_join(LINE_JOIN_MAP[vmobject.joint_type])
ctx.set_line_cap(CAP_STYLE_MAP[vmobject.cap_style])
```
That

We also discussed this subject in issue #4979 where I traced the problem to the same source, though without a good idea of the correct fix.

It looks like `CapStyleType.AUTO` and this behavior has existed since cap styles were introduced two years ago. However, I suspect that was just done to copy the existing behavior of `LineJointType.AUTO` which was implemented the year before by in #3016. Seems like the choice to make `AUTO` mean "do the same thing as before" was made by @behackl in commit 7c7d0b3.

I think it would probably be fine to outright remove `AUTO`, though maybe in a future version with a notice about it in the release before it.

If we really want to keep `AUTO`, perhaps we could define a global or renderer-level default value for line joints and cap styles (probably defaulting to `ROUND` and `BUTT`) which any `AUTO` values then map to. That would let the user define their own auto values.

How do other graphics libraries handle this?

Superseded by #5016 -- I think the breaking change here wasn't entirely worth it, and I preferred the approach there. We might still want to sit down and think about an overall cleaner solution for the cap styles... we'll have to do so either way when we detach renderer-specific information from mobjects. Thanks, regardless, for your efforts here!

## Enhancement proposal
Currently, Manim stores the point data for `VMobjects` as a flat list of points. This is not representative at all of how `VMobjects` are actually structured, i.e. as composite bezier curves. In fact, every four points (three for OpenGL) form the points defining a cubic/bezier curve, yet they are currently not explicitly grouped together. Furthermore, the data of which points form what paths is not stored, and Manim instead spends a significant amount of time every frame checking whether for each pair of consecutive bezier curves, their end and start points are close e

A possible approach is to have a `Bezier` dataclass, then having the `points` array be an array of these dataclasses. This easily extends to allow different path components. If they are made immutable, it will help with caching. However, this might cause overhead when operating on points (I think it would be perfect, if not for that problem).

One possible approach is to have components be subclasses of numpy arrays. Pointwise functions can still be applied directly with numpy through `apply_along_axis`. This could retain speed while semantically splitting up data. Needs more investigation.

I have recently been thinking about this. Calculations of things like subpaths, bounding boxes* and unit normals could be memoized and grouped inside a separate object. For `Mobject`s, it could be something like `MobjectPoints`. For `VMobject`s, it could be a subclass of `MobjectPoints` called `VMobjectPoints`.
